claims.text: The baseline material is a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy containing at least three additional elements, with each constituent present at 5–35 at%.
Approximately 6 at% aluminum is added to the baseline alloy.
Homogenization ensures an even elemental distribution in the alloy.
Adding approximately 6 at% aluminum promotes formation of nanoscale, coherent L12-type precipitates.
The anticipated L12 precipitates are Ni3Al-like.
Homogenization followed by solution treatment promotes formation of the anticipated L12 precipitates.
Coherent L12 precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the precipitates produces dispersion strengthening at elevated temperature.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have greater yield strength at approximately 800 °C than the corresponding alloy without aluminum.
The proposed intervention applies when every constituent, including aluminum, remains within 5–35 at%.
The strengthening intervention depends on processing conditions being optimized to promote L12 precipitation.
A significant strengthening effect is expected, while the exact percentage improvement, including whether it reaches approximately 15%, is uncertain.
The aluminum-modified alloy is implicitly expected to improve creep resistance at 800 °C relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies improved yield strength, but the falsification rule also requires improved creep resistance; failure to improve creep is therefore treated as falsifying an outcome that the main hypothesis does not explicitly predict.

The baseline is called an 'identical ... alloy composition' while also being specified as lacking the approximately 6 at% aluminum present after intervention. The intended meaning is likely identical processing and otherwise corresponding composition, but the literal composition cannot be identical.
